21st Century Tech on the Covid Front Line

By: John Webb | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look into how cutting edge technologies are being harnesses in the battle against SARS-CoV-2.

Unique Selling Point:
Hospitals and frontline medical staff are the forefront of the struggle against Covid19, but 21st century technologies like Artificial Intelligence and high-powered X-rays are being deployed behind the scenes to bolster our ability to counter this unseen enemy. We get a first-hand insight into one such technology, the so-called Diamond Light Source. It's described as pure light, billions of times brighter than the sun, able to deliver X-Rays of such clarity that researchers are able to watch molecules interacting with the microscopic building blocks that constitute this new Coronavirus.

Summary:
Diamond Light Source is at the centre of a global crowd-sourcing experiment. Its owners have made the technology available to scientists all over the world who believe they have the right recipe for a compound capable of neutralising the virus. For a small fee, they're able to submit the molecular make-up to the Diamond team who then create the experiment required to test the interaction between the compound and some of the virus's constituent parts. That interaction is observed in the high-quality x-rays delivered by this high-intensity light-source. It's hoped that this unprecedented crowd sourcing initiative will deliver a compound capable of fighting the virus which can then be manufactured and tested as a new drug.

Allied to this is another example of how technology is being used to assist in the fight against Covid19: Artificial Intelligence and its ability to process what's know as "Big Data". It's an application of machine learning that allows researchers to produce accurate models on the impact and behavior of the virus at a speed previously unheard of. At Wits, academics and researchers have built a detailed Covid dashboard that provides the most accurate picture available of the spread of the virus and impact of the disease it causes, Covid19. Crucially, using complex mathematics, it's able to predict future patterns allowing governments to shape policy befitting the reality. It also provides a useful example of the relationship between the technology and the humans using it.

Script:


Script: Coronavirus and AI

VO: And that is what we’re dealing with: something invisible to the naked eye with a desire to replicate. 7sec

VO: Coronaviruses - like the one that causes Covid19 – have multiple parts. An outer protein casing, called the viral envelope, covers the genetic material. They gain access to human cells and, once inside, they go to work replicating and assembling themselves, turning the cell into what you might call a “virus factory”. 26sec

VO: And that process repeated over and over again is what emptied our streets, shut our schools and businesses and confined us to our homes for weeks on end. And the chance of it doing so again, remains a constant threat. 14 seconds, plus 2 seconds

VO: And right now, our best defence is social distancing and obsessive hygiene. But that’s not where the fightback ends. 9sec

VO: The global scientific community is mounting a 21st century response. And one of the most obvious examples is by harnessing the power of artificial intelligence. 10seca

VO: As someone tapped into the world of scientific innovation, Simon Gear, understands the edge AI and machine learning provide in the battle against Covid19. And it’s about more than just processing enormous amounts of data. 15sec

VO: AI and machine learning have been vital tools in medical science for some time, and their contribution to the fight against Covid19 is already significant. From developing track and trace technologies for cell phone applications to analysing billions of drug combinations in the search for a therapy. 18sec

VO: Bruce Mellado is a physics Professor at Wits University. He led the team that built this comprehensive Covid19 dashboard. It’s crucial work relying heavily on AI to provide a glimpse of the future by monitoring almost every country in the world. 16sec

VO: It’s a monumental task: using complex mathematics to make predictions about the impact of a virus we’re still learning about on societies that all respond differently to the threat. A task that greatly benefits from AI. 14sec

VO: But, the relationship between researcher and intelligent machine is a two-way street. Left to run free, it would be a mistake to believe AI would provide the silver bullet to end this crisis. 11sec

VO: But, it remains pivotal to a scientific response trying to achieve the best possible result at high speed. And there’s an unfolding global collaboration that epitomises that better than most. It’s a prime example of what the Americans might call “can do-ism”. 16sec

VO: President John F Kennedy’s speech more than 50 years ago best describes something called a “Moon Shot”: an ambitious project aimed at achieving a monumental goal. 12sec

VO: And, that is what’s happening in this extraordinary building in the UK. This is Diamond Light Source, one of the most advanced scientific facilities in the world. It’s what’s known as a synchrotron; the focal point of a project dubbed the COVID Moon Shot and technology so advanced it’ll make your head spin. 20sec

VO: Billions of electrons are fired into three particle accelerators. The first two speed up the electrons until they’re traveling at almost the speed of light. In the third the electrons pass through magnetic arrays that make them emit intensely bright light - up to ten billion times brighter than the sun.
18sec

VO: That light, in forms that include x-rays, is then directed into these experimental labs where scientists use it to study the structure of matter itself. And it turns out, that’s very useful in a pandemic. 14sec

VO: South African-born, Frank von Delft, is an Oxford Professor and scientist at Diamond Light Source one of several institutions collaborating on Covid-Moon Shot. He and his colleagues are trying to understand the structure of the novel coronavirus and how it interacts with molecules that might result in a new anti-viral drug. 19sec

VO: The team synthesised hundreds of crystals of the virus’s main protease. That’s a protein that is critical to the virus’s self-replication machinery. 10sec

VO: A single protein crystal is x-rayed from every angle and the 3600 two-dimensional images are then combined to form a three-dimensional model of the protein’s structure. By understanding this structure, the MoonShot team can find ways of interfering with the virus’s ultimate objective: to reproduce. 21sec

VO: The “spanner” is a chemical compound that will bind to a particular part of the protein and inhibit its function. 7sec

VO: Diamond has already identified 71 of the most promising candidates: fragments that could form the building blocks for antiviral drugs that might eventually stop the viral ‘machine’ from working. But the next challenge is to piece them together: to design the molecules that will make up those antiviral drugs. And to achieve that, the collaborators did something a little unusual: they asked for help. 24sec

VO: It was a masterstroke: 250 scientists have so far responded with 4500 molecule designs. The technology at Diamond will be used to test a thousand of the most promising designs to see if they have the desired effect on the areas of the virus identified for attack. Professor von Delft is cautious about making predictions, but his gut instinct says they’re on the right track. 24sec

VO: So, if there is a silver lining to this cloud perhaps it’s the extraordinary collaboration with which this crisis is being met. And, that might just stand us in good stead when others come our way. 14sec

Ends.
